question:
Consider the following statements about the Buddhist Councils:

1. The Third Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka.

2. The Fourth Council was held under Kanishka at Kundalavana in Kashmir.

3. The First Council was organised by Bimbisara at Vaishali.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statements 1 and 2 are correct because Ashoka held the Third Council at Pataliputra and Kanishka the Fourth at Kundalavana in Kashmir, but statement 3 is false since the First Council was organised by Ajatashatru at Rajagriha (प्रथम संगीति — राजगृह, अजातशत्रु)

 

• Bimbisara, wrongly named in statement 3, was an earlier Haryanka king and a friend of the Buddha who died before him, whereas the first council met only after the Buddha's death.

 

• Vaishali, also wrongly named, was the venue of the Second Council a century later and not of the First.

 

• Such mixed true and false statements about patrons and venues are a favourite SSC trap.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa presided at the Third Council and Vasumitra at the Fourth.

 

• Ashoka sent Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka and other lands after the Third Council.

 

• Kanishka's capital was Purushapura, modern Peshawar.

 

• Ashoka's own rock edicts and pillar edicts do not describe the Councils, which are known mainly from Buddhist chronicles of Sri Lanka.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 wrongly gives Bimbisara and Vaishali for the First Council, and this pair also drops the correct statement 1 about Ashoka at Pataliputra, so it cannot be accepted.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): That combination takes the false statement 3 with statement 1 but ignores the true statement 2 about Kanishka and Kashmir, and the First Council was at Rajagriha, so it fails.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Marking every statement as correct fails because statement 3 is untrue; Ajatashatru, not Bimbisara, organised the First Council at Rajagriha.

question: Which Buddhist Council was held in Kashmir under the patronage of Kanishka?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Fourth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Fourth Buddhist Council was held at Kundalavana (near Srinagar), Kashmir, under the patronage of the Kushana king Kanishka (चतुर्थ बौद्ध संगीति — कश्मीर, कनिष्क)

 

• The Fourth Council met at Kundalavana near Srinagar in Kashmir under the Kushana king Kanishka, with Vasumitra as chairman, and the notes link it with the rise of Mahayana.

 

• Kanishka was among the greatest patrons of Buddhism in India, building stupas and supporting scholars such as Ashvaghosha, Nagarjuna and the physician Charaka according to tradition.

 

• Because it was held in the north-west, far from Magadha, the council reflects the spread of Buddhism along the trade routes to Central Asia.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kanishka's reign is associated with the Shaka era that begins in 78 AD.

 

• Gandhara and Mathura schools of art flourished in his time.

 

• Ashvaghosha, who wrote the Buddhacharita, is linked with his court.

 

• Tradition says Kanishka erected a great stupa at Purushapura, whose remains were seen by the Chinese pilgrims Fa-Hien and Xuanzang.

 

NOTE

 

• First (Option 2): The First Council was held at Rajagriha in Magadha in 483 BC, not in Kashmir. Its patron was the Haryanka king Ajatashatru, so it does not match the description.

 

• Second (Option 3): The Second Council was held at Vaishali under Kalashoka and Subhakami. It happened in the Gangetic plain and long before the Kushana age, so it is not the Kashmir council.

 

• Third (Option 4): The Third Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka and Moggaliputta Tissa. Pataliputra is in Bihar, in eastern India, so it is not the council of Kashmir.

question:
Match the Buddhist Councils with their venues:

(a) First Council

(b) Second Council

(c) Third Council

(d) Fourth Council

(i) Pataliputra

(ii) Kundalavana, Kashmir

(iii) Rajagriha

(iv) Vaishali
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The four councils were held at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Kundalavana (Kashmir) in that order, under the patrons Ajatashatru, Kalashoka, Ashoka and Kanishka (चार बौद्ध संगीतियाँ — राजगृह, वैशाली, पाटलिपुत्र, कुण्डलवन)

 

• The dates in the notes are 483 BC, 383 BC, 250 BC and the Kushana age, which also give the order in which the venues must appear.

 

• The first three councils were in the Magadha region, showing the early centre of Buddhism, while the fourth moved to Kashmir with the Kushanas.

 

• Memorise venue, patron and chairman together as a single row.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• SSC 2025 asked students to identify the correctly matched Buddhist council and its location.

 

• The chairmen were Mahakasyapa, Subhakami, Moggaliputta Tissa and Vasumitra.

 

• Rajagriha, Vaishali and Pataliputra were all in the Magadha-Vajji region of the Gangetic plain.

 

• The meeting places show how the centre of Buddhist activity moved from the middle Ganga plain to the north-west under the Kushanas.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-iii, c-ii, d-i (Option 1): Reversing the venues by giving Vaishali to the First Council and Pataliputra to the Second leaves none of the four pairs correct, so the option fails completely.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 2): Placing the Second Council at Pataliputra and the Third at Vaishali is wrong, since the Second was at Vaishali under Kalashoka and the Third at Pataliputra under Ashoka.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): Giving the First Council to Pataliputra and the Third to Rajagriha interchanges two pairs, whereas the First was at Rajagriha and the Third at Pataliputra.

question:
Match the Buddhist Councils with their chairmen:

(a) First Council

(b) Second Council

(c) Third Council

(d) Fourth Council

(i) Vasumitra

(ii) Mahakasyapa

(iii) Moggaliputta Tissa

(iv) Subhakami
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-ii, b-iv, c-iii, d-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The chairmen were Mahakasyapa (First), Subhakami (Second), Moggaliputta Tissa (Third) and Vasumitra (Fourth), who presided at Rajagriha, Vaishali, Pataliputra and Kundalavana respectively (संगीतियों के अध्यक्ष — महाकश्यप, सुभकामी, मोग्गलिपुत्त तिस्स, वसुमित्र)

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa was Ashoka's spiritual adviser and is credited with the Kathavatthu, a work of the Abhidhamma Pitaka.

 

• Vasumitra is traditionally said to have been assisted by Ashvaghosha at the Fourth Council.

 

• Pairing each chairman with his council and patron makes such match questions easy.

 

• The Third Council's chairman Moggaliputta Tissa and the Fourth's Vasumitra belong to different centuries, since Ashoka ruled in the third century BC and Kanishka in the early centuries AD.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The patrons of the four councils were Ajatashatru, Kalashoka, Ashoka and Kanishka.

 

• Ashvaghosha is traditionally named as Vasumitra's deputy at the Fourth Council.

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa's council is linked with the sending of missions abroad.

 

• Subhakami is spelt Sabakami or Sabbakami in some books, so the spelling in an SSC option may vary slightly.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iv, b-ii, c-i, d-iii (Option 2): Reversing the first two pairs and the last two puts every chairman against the wrong council, so Mahakasyapa and Subhakami and the later two are all misplaced.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i (Option 3): Getting the first and fourth pairs right but swapping the middle ones fails, since Subhakami chaired the Second Council at Vaishali and Moggaliputta Tissa the Third.

 

• a-i, b-iv, c-iii, d-ii (Option 4): Giving Vasumitra to the First Council and Mahakasyapa to the Fourth reverses the real order, because Mahakasyapa belongs to the earliest council and Vasumitra to the latest.

question: Which of the following correctly gives the chronological order of the four Buddhist Councils by their venues?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajagriha - Vaishali - Pataliputra - Kundalavana.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The order is Rajagriha (First, 483 BC), Vaishali (Second, 383 BC), Pataliputra (Third, 250 BC) and Kundalavana (Fourth, Kushana period) (संगीतियों का कालक्रम)

 

• The correct sequence is Rajagriha (First, 483 BC), Vaishali (Second, 383 BC), Pataliputra (Third, 250 BC) and Kundalavana (Fourth, Kushana age).

 

• The intervals show that the first two councils were a century apart, the Mauryan council came about 130 years after the second, and the Kushana council came much later.

 

• Ajatashatru, Kalashoka, Ashoka and Kanishka are the patrons in this order, and tying venues to patrons helps to fix the sequence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda and Mauryan dynasties ruled Magadha in that order.

 

• Ashoka's reign (c. 268-232 BC) saw the spread of Buddhism outside India.

 

• Kanishka belonged to the Kushana dynasty, which ruled in north-west India.

 

• The interval between the Second and Third Councils is about 130 years, while that between the Third and Fourth is more than three centuries.

 

NOTE

 

• Vaishali - Rajagriha - Kundalavana - Pataliputra (Option 1): This option puts Vaishali before Rajagriha and Kashmir before Pataliputra, so the order of the first two and the last two councils is inverted. It cannot be the chronological sequence.

 

• Rajagriha - Pataliputra - Vaishali - Kundalavana (Option 3): This option places Pataliputra before Vaishali, but the Second Council at Vaishali (383 BC) was held well before Ashoka's Pataliputra council (250 BC), so the middle pair is reversed.

 

• Pataliputra - Rajagriha - Vaishali - Kundalavana (Option 4): This option starts with Pataliputra, which was the Third Council. The earliest council was at Rajagriha, so a sequence that opens with Pataliputra cannot be correct.

question: The Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra, organised by Ashoka, was presided over by:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Moggaliputta Tissa.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Third Buddhist Council (c. 250 BC) at Pataliputra was presided over by Moggaliputta Tissa under the patronage of Ashoka (मोग्गलिपुत्त तिस्स — तृतीय बौद्ध संगीति, पाटलिपुत्र)

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa presided over the Third Council at Pataliputra (c. 250 BC), organised by Ashoka, and is associated with the Abhidhamma Pitaka and the purification of the Sangha.

 

• Tradition says Ashoka had heretical monks expelled and then asked Moggaliputta Tissa to question the monks on the true doctrine, which resulted in a formal statement of the Theravada position.

 

• After this council missions were sent to many regions, including Sri Lanka where Ashoka's son Mahendra established Buddhism.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kathavatthu is traditionally credited to Moggaliputta Tissa.

 

• Ashoka's Schism Edict warned monks and nuns against dividing the Sangha.

 

• Pataliputra was the Mauryan capital, on the Ganga near modern Patna.

 

• Ashoka is said to have sent nine missions after the Third Council, among them to Kashmir-Gandhara, Mahisamandala (Mysore) and Suvarnabhumi.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahakasyapa (Option 1): Mahakasyapa presided over the First Council at Rajagriha shortly after the Buddha's death, about two centuries before Ashoka. He cannot have been the chairman at Pataliputra.

 

• Vasumitra (Option 2): Vasumitra presided at the Fourth Council in Kashmir under Kanishka, in the Kushana period. He lived long after Ashoka, so he cannot have chaired the Third Council.

 

• Subhakami (Option 4): Subhakami was the chairman of the Second Council at Vaishali under Kalashoka. That meeting occurred more than a century before the Third Council at Pataliputra.

question: Which of the following is a feature of Mahayana Buddhism?
option_1: Rejection of all images of the Buddha
option_2: Strict adherence to the original simple teachings alone
option_3: Emphasis only on individual salvation of monks
option_4: Worship of Buddha images and belief in Bodhisattvas
solution_text:
The correct answer is Worship of Buddha images and belief in Bodhisattvas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Mahayana (the 'new way of thinking') accepted image worship of the Buddha and the idea of Bodhisattvas, and is associated with the Fourth Council under Kanishka (महायान — मूर्ति पूजा, बोधिसत्व)

 

• Mahayana, the new way of thinking, accepted image worship of the Buddha and the Bodhisattva ideal, and the notes link its rise with the Fourth Council under Kanishka.

 

• Because it encouraged making Buddha images, it led to the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art, which replaced the earlier symbols.

 

• Hinayana, as the notes use the term, stands for the older tradition that follows the Buddha's original teachings as spread by Ashoka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahayana means the great vehicle and Hinayana the lesser vehicle.

 

• Mahayana travelled to China, Korea and Japan, while Theravada reached Sri Lanka and South-East Asia.

 

• Ashvaghosha and Nagarjuna are famous Mahayana thinkers.

 

• The Bodhisattva ideal of Mahayana is described in the Jataka-like stories of compassion and in the Prajnaparamita literature.

 

NOTE

 

• Rejection of all images of the Buddha (Option 1): Rejecting all images describes early Buddhism before the Kushana age, when the Buddha was shown only by symbols such as the wheel and the tree. Mahayana did the opposite and encouraged images.

 

• Strict adherence to the original simple teachings alone (Option 2): Strict adherence to the original simple teachings alone describes the older school, called Hinayana in the notes. Mahayana added new ideas such as Bodhisattvas, so it is not a feature of the new school.

 

• Emphasis only on individual salvation of monks (Option 3): Concentrating only on the monks' personal salvation describes the older arhat ideal. Mahayana stressed compassion and the salvation of all beings through the Bodhisattva, which is a different emphasis.

question: The Buddhist literature in the Pali language is known as the Tri-Pitaka. The term 'Tri-Pitaka' literally means:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Three baskets.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tri-Pitaka (Tipitaka) literally means three baskets, the collection of Buddhist texts in the Pali language (त्रिपिटक — तीन पिटारे)

 

• Tri-Pitaka means three baskets, and the name is given to the collection of Buddhist texts in the Pali language: Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma.

 

• The notes say that the texts were collected and compiled roughly five hundred years after the Buddha's death, though they preserve earlier oral teaching.

 

• The word pitaka (basket) is believed to refer to the baskets in which the palm-leaf manuscripts were stored.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pali canon survives mainly in the Theravada countries such as Sri Lanka and Myanmar.

 

• The Tripitaka was first written down in Sri Lanka in the first century BC.

 

• Mahayana texts such as the Lotus Sutra are generally in Sanskrit.

 

• The Buddhist canon in Pali is often called Tipitaka, and Buddhist texts in Sanskrit often use the form Tripitaka.

 

NOTE

 

• Three jewels (Option 2): Three jewels is the meaning of Tri Ratna, namely the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha. It is a different Buddhist triad about objects of refuge, not about the canon.

 

• Three paths (Option 3): Three paths has no standing as the meaning of the term. The Buddhist path is the Eightfold Path with eight limbs, and the Tripitaka refers to texts, not to paths.

 

• Three vehicles (Option 4): Three vehicles would refer to the later Buddhist schools often called Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana. The word Pitaka means basket and has no relation to vehicle (yana).

question: The Vinaya Pitaka of the Tri-Pitaka primarily contains:
option_3: Rules of discipline for Buddhist monasteries
option_4: Stories of the Buddha's previous births
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rules of discipline for Buddhist monasteries.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vinaya Pitaka contains the rules of discipline followed in Buddhist monasteries; it was recited by Upali at the First Council (विनय पिटक — मठ के अनुशासन के नियम)

 

• The Vinaya Pitaka contains the rules of discipline for the monks and nuns of the Sangha, covering matters such as admission, begging for alms, dress, residence and punishment of offenders.

 

• It was recited at the First Council by Upali, who was regarded as the most skilled monk in monastic discipline.

 

• These rules explain how the Sangha was run and why it lasted for centuries as an organised institution.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Vinaya includes the Patimokkha, the code recited by the monks twice a month.

 

• Vinaya is the Pali word for discipline.

 

• SSC 2025 asked a Vinaya Pitaka question in Delhi Police and other papers with options on monastic rules.

 

• The Vinaya Pitaka also records the rules for the rainy season retreat (vassa), when monks stayed at one place for three months.

 

NOTE

 

• Sermons of the Buddha (Option 1): The sermons of the Buddha are collected in the Sutta Pitaka, which was recited by Ananda at the First Council. The Vinaya Pitaka deals instead with the conduct of monks and nuns.

 

• Philosophical principles of Buddhism (Option 2): Philosophical principles of Buddhism are discussed in the Abhidhamma Pitaka, which was prepared at the Third Council under Ashoka. The Vinaya Pitaka is about discipline and not about doctrine.

 

• Stories of the Buddha's previous births (Option 4): Stories of the Buddha's previous births are the Jataka tales, which are included in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka. They are not part of the code of monastic discipline.

question: Which Pitaka is the largest of the three and is called the 'encyclopaedia of Buddhism'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sutta Pitaka.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sutta Pitaka is the largest of the three baskets; it contains the Buddha's sermons and teachings along with the story of his life and is called the 'encyclopaedia of Buddhism', associated with Ananda (सुत्त पिटक — बौद्ध धर्म का विश्वकोश)

 

• The Sutta Pitaka is the largest of the three baskets and is called the encyclopaedia of Buddhism because it contains the sermons and teachings of the Buddha and the story of his life; Ananda recited it at the First Council.

 

• It is arranged into five collections called Nikayas: Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, Anguttara and Khuddaka.

 

• The Khuddaka Nikaya includes the Dhammapada and the Jataka, which are the most popular books of the canon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Anguttara Nikaya contains the list of the sixteen Mahajanapadas.

 

• The Dhammapada is a collection of moral verses and a favourite of general readers.

 

• Ananda is famed as the Buddha's attendant with a remarkable memory.

 

• The Majjhima Nikaya (middle-length discourses) and the Digha Nikaya (long discourses) are two other collections of the Sutta Pitaka.

 

NOTE

 

• Vinaya Pitaka (Option 2): The Vinaya Pitaka contains the code of discipline for monks and is smaller than the Sutta Pitaka. It is not called the encyclopaedia of Buddhism.

 

• Abhidhamma Pitaka (Option 3): The Abhidhamma Pitaka discusses Buddhist philosophy and was prepared at the Third Council. It is a technical text and not the large collection of sermons.

 

• Jataka Pitaka (Option 4): A Jataka Pitaka does not exist as one of the three baskets. The Jatakas are birth stories of the Buddha and form a part of the Khuddaka Nikaya within the Sutta Pitaka.

question:
Match the Pitakas of the Tri-Pitaka with their features:

(a) Vinaya Pitaka

(b) Sutta Pitaka

(c) Abhidhamma Pitaka

(i) Philosophical principles of Buddhism

(ii) Associated with Ananda; Buddha's sermons

(iii) Associated with Upali; monastic discipline
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Vinaya goes with Upali and monastic discipline, Sutta with Ananda and the sermons, and Abhidhamma with the philosophical principles prepared at the Third Council (त्रिपिटक — विनय, सुत्त, अभिधम्म का मिलान)

 

• Upali and Ananda recited their baskets at the First Council, which links each Pitaka to a person and to an event.

 

• All three baskets are in Pali, so the whole canon is called the Pali canon.

 

• Only one of the options matches all three baskets correctly.

 

• Compilation of the Tripitaka took centuries: the Vinaya and Sutta were first fixed at Rajagriha, the Abhidhamma later, and the whole canon was written down in Sri Lanka.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sutta Pitaka is the largest of the three baskets.

 

• The notes call the Abhidhamma also a biography of monks who lived in Ashoka's time.

 

• The Vinaya Pitaka is divided into Sutta Vibhanga, Khandhaka and Parivara.

 

• The Abhidhamma Pitaka is regarded as the later basket, and its contents are not held to be sermons delivered directly by the Buddha in the Sutta style.

 

NOTE

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-i (Option 1): Interchanging the Vinaya and Sutta Pitakas, by giving Ananda to the Vinaya and Upali to the Sutta, is wrong because Upali is tied to monastic discipline and Ananda to the sermons.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-ii (Option 2): Giving philosophy to the Sutta Pitaka and Ananda to the Abhidhamma is a mix-up; the Sutta Pitaka holds the sermons and Ananda recited it, while the Abhidhamma is the philosophical basket.

 

• a-i, b-ii, c-iii (Option 3): Allotting philosophy to the Vinaya and Upali to the Abhidhamma mismatches all three baskets, since the Vinaya concerns discipline and Upali's recitation.

question: The Abhidhamma Pitaka of the Buddhist canon mainly deals with:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Philosophical principles of Buddhism.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with the philosophical principles of Buddhism and was prepared at the Third Council under Ashoka (अभिधम्म पिटक — दार्शनिक सिद्धांत)

 

• The Abhidhamma Pitaka deals with the philosophical principles of Buddhism and was prepared at the Third Council under Ashoka; the notes also describe it as a biography of the monks of Ashoka's time.

 

• Abhidhamma means higher doctrine, and its style is analytical, analysing mind, matter and the path to Nirvana, in contrast to the narrative style of the Sutta Pitaka.

 

• Moggaliputta Tissa, who presided at that council, is credited with the Kathavatthu, a text refuting rival schools.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Theravada tradition has seven books in the Abhidhamma Pitaka.

 

• The Third Council was held around 250 BC at Pataliputra.

 

• The three baskets together form the Pali canon.

 

• The Abhidhamma's analysis of mind and matter has influenced Buddhist psychology and meditation teaching in Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand.

 

• Buddhist teachers in Sri Lanka and Myanmar still recite the Abhidhamma on special occasions, and it is studied in monastic examinations.

 

NOTE

 

• Rules for monastic life (Option 1): Rules for monastic life are the subject of the Vinaya Pitaka, which was recited by Upali. The Abhidhamma deals with doctrine and philosophy instead.

 

• Biography of the Buddha only (Option 3): A biography of the Buddha alone is not the content of the Abhidhamma. His life and sermons are found mainly in the Sutta Pitaka, and the Abhidhamma is a philosophical work.

 

• Rules of royal governance (Option 4): Rules of royal governance belong to works like the Arthashastra of Kautilya and not to any Buddhist Pitaka. The Buddhist canon deals with religion, ethics and monastic law.

question: The 'Jataka' stories, written in the Pali language, are tales about the previous births of:
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Buddha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Jataka tales are stories of the previous births of the Buddha (as a Bodhisattva), written in Pali (जातक कथाएँ — बुद्ध के पूर्व जन्म)

 

• The Jataka tales relate the previous births of the Buddha as a Bodhisattva, when he took various animal and human forms and practised virtues such as generosity and compassion; they are in Pali.

 

• They are part of the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka and are among the most popular Buddhist writings.

 

• SSC has asked this question more than once, so remember Jataka means birth story and is connected with Buddha.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Jataka scenes were carved on the railings of Bharhut and Sanchi stupas and painted at Ajanta.

 

• The tales reflect trade, towns and village life in early India, so historians use them as sources.

 

• Jain literature has its own life stories of the Tirthankaras, but not Jatakas.

 

• The Jataka tales number about five hundred and fifty in the commonly accepted collection, with stories such as the Vessantara Jataka and the Chhaddanta Jataka.

 

NOTE

 

• Mahavira (Option 1): Mahavira's earlier births are described in Jain tradition, which has its own narrative literature in Prakrit. The Jataka collection, however, is a Buddhist work about the Bodhisattva.

 

• Rama (Option 2): Rama is the hero of the Ramayana and is regarded in Hinduism as an avatar of Vishnu. His story is told in the epic and Puranas, not in the Jatakas.

 

• Krishna (Option 4): Krishna is a Hindu deity whose life is described in the Mahabharata and the Puranas. His stories are not part of the Pali Jataka collection.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Tri-Pitaka:

1. The Vinaya Pitaka contains the rules of monastic discipline.

2. The Sutta Pitaka is the largest of the three Pitakas.

3. The Abhidhamma Pitaka was prepared at the Third Buddhist Council.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The three Pitaka statements are all correct: Vinaya holds the monastic rules, Sutta is the largest basket and the Abhidhamma was prepared at the Third Council (त्रिपिटक — विनय, सुत्त, अभिधम्म)

 

• Tying each basket to its reciter (Upali for the Vinaya, Ananda for the Sutta) and to its subject (discipline, sermons, philosophy) helps to eliminate wrong options quickly.

 

• Together the three baskets form the Pali canon, which the Theravada tradition has preserved.

 

• No statement here needs to be rejected.

 

• A practical way to check such statements is to ask who recited the basket, what it contains and when it was fixed; each of the three statements here passes all three tests.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sutta Pitaka is called the encyclopaedia of Buddhism because of its size and range.

 

• The Abhidhamma Pitaka is an analytic treatment of the doctrine.

 

• Texts were passed on orally for generations before being written.

 

• The word Dhammapada means the path of the Dhamma, and its verses are frequently quoted in Buddhist ethics.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Taking only statements 1 and 2 leaves out statement 3, which is also correct, since the notes say the Abhidhamma Pitaka was prepared at the Third Council.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Taking only statements 2 and 3 leaves out statement 1, but the Vinaya Pitaka does contain the rules followed in Buddhist monasteries, so the omission is a mistake.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): Taking only statements 1 and 3 leaves out statement 2, although the Sutta Pitaka is the biggest of the three baskets and is called the encyclopaedia of Buddhism.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa:

1. They are ancient Buddhist chronicles of Sri Lanka.

2. They are written in the Pali language.

3. They describe the spread of Buddhism in Sri Lanka under the patronage of Ashoka.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are ancient Pali chronicles of Sri Lanka that describe how Buddhism arrived and was established there under Ashoka's royal patronage, so all three statements stand (दीपवंश और महावंश — श्रीलंका के पालि इतिहास ग्रंथ)

 

• They tell of the mission of Mahendra and Sanghamitra and of the conversion of the Sri Lankan king, giving details that complement Ashoka's own edicts.

 

• They are therefore valuable sources for Mauryan history and for the history of Theravada Buddhism.

 

• The question follows the 'Important Points' box in the notes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Mahendra is traditionally described as Ashoka's son, and Sanghamitra as his daughter.

 

• The Bodhi tree sapling brought by Sanghamitra was planted at Anuradhapura.

 

• The Mahavamsa was composed in verse in Pali.

 

• Sri Lanka was the first country outside India to receive Buddhism, in the reign of Devanampiya Tissa, a contemporary of Ashoka.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 1 and 2 (Option 1): Selecting only the first two statements overlooks statement 3, yet these chronicles do describe the spread of Buddhism in Sri Lanka with Ashoka's patronage.

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 2): Selecting only the last two statements ignores statement 1, although they are indeed ancient Buddhist chronicles of Sri Lanka. Statement 1 is therefore as correct as the other two, which makes this combination incomplete.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 4): Selecting statements 1 and 3 alone disregards statement 2, even though the notes say both works are written in the Pali language.

question: In the structure of a Buddhist stupa, the large hemispherical dome is known as the:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Anda.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The large hemispherical dome of a stupa is called the Anda (egg); it symbolises the universe and often covers the sacred relics of the Buddha or a monk (अण्ड — स्तूप का अर्धगोलाकार गुंबद)

 

• The Anda is the large hemispherical dome of the stupa, symbolising the universe and covering the sacred relic chamber; it stands on the raised Medhi and is crowned by the Harmika.

 

• A stupa began as a burial mound for the relics of the Buddha or of revered monks, and over time it grew into the central object of Buddhist worship.

 

• The Great Stupa at Sanchi is the best-known surviving example showing all six parts named in the notes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Pradakshina Patha is the circumambulation path, the Vedika the railing and the Torana the gateway.

 

• Sanchi's gateways carry Jataka scenes and events of the Buddha's life.

 

• The Dhamekh Stupa at Sarnath is another important stupa.

 

• The earliest stupas were mounds of earth and brick, and Ashoka is said to have redistributed relics of the Buddha under many stupas.

 

NOTE

 

• Medhi (Option 2): The Medhi is the raised circular platform or terrace that supports the dome. It forms the base of the structure and is not itself the dome.

 

• Harmika (Option 3): The Harmika is the small square railing-like structure on top of the dome and is regarded as the symbolic abode of the gods. It is a crowning element and not the dome.

 

• Vedika (Option 4): The Vedika is the railing or enclosure surrounding the sacred area. It marks off the stupa's precinct and is not the hemisphere of the dome.

question: The small square railing-like structure placed on top of the Anda of a stupa, regarded as the symbolic abode of the gods, is the:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Harmika.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• On top of the dome sits the Harmika, a small square railing-like enclosure regarded as the symbolic abode of the gods (हर्मिका — देवताओं का प्रतीकात्मक निवास)

 

• From the centre of the Harmika rose a mast carrying stone umbrellas (chhatras), which represent honour and the sovereignty of the Buddha.

 

• Of the six parts named in the notes, the Harmika is the topmost element.

 

• The other five parts are the Anda, Medhi, Pradakshina Patha, Vedika and Torana.

 

• Together with the Anda, the Harmika forms the part of the stupa where the sacred relic casket was placed, which is why the notes link it with the abode of the gods.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• SSC 2025 asked a statement-based question on the Harmika and the stupa.

 

• The Harmika form later influenced the finials of temple spires.

 

• Relics were kept in a chamber within the dome.

 

• The Harmika-and-umbrella arrangement is seen in the Sanchi Great Stupa, which preserves its stone umbrella on a central pillar.

 

NOTE

 

• Torana (Option 1): The Torana is the ornamental gateway that gives entry to the stupa complex. It stands at the entrances in the Vedika, not at the top of the dome.

 

• Pradakshina Patha (Option 2): The Pradakshina Patha is the pathway used for walking round the stupa, so it lies at ground level around the structure and not on the dome.

 

• Medhi (Option 4): The Medhi is the raised circular platform that supports the Anda. It is at the base, which is the opposite of an element placed on top of the dome.

question:
Match the parts of a stupa with their descriptions:

(a) Medhi

(b) Pradakshina Patha

(c) Vedika

(d) Torana

(i) Railing or enclosure

(ii) Ornamental gateway

(iii) Path for circumambulation

(iv) Raised circular platform supporting the dome
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iv, b-iii, c-i, d-ii.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Medhi is the raised circular platform, the Pradakshina Patha the circumambulation path, the Vedika the railing and the Torana the ornamental gateway (स्तूप के भाग — मेधि, प्रदक्षिणा पथ, वेदिका, तोरण)

 

• The remaining two parts are the Anda (dome) and the Harmika (square railing on top), completing the six parts named in the notes.

 

• A visitor enters through the Torana, walks clockwise along the Pradakshina Patha and looks up at the Anda and the Harmika.

 

• Each part is distinct in function, so the matches are easy to fix.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sanchi's four Toranas date from the Satavahana period.

 

• Bharhut is famous for its Vedika.

 

• Stupas were also built by Jains and later by Hindus in some regions as shrine forms.

 

• The Sanchi Torana carved with scenes from the Jatakas and life of the Buddha is a favourite subject for SSC art and architecture questions.

 

NOTE

 

• a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i (Option 1): Swapping all four pairs, by giving the walking path to the platform and the railing to the gateway, leaves no pair right.

 

• a-iv, b-i, c-iii, d-ii (Option 2): Matching the Medhi and the Torana correctly but swapping the Pradakshina Patha with the Vedika fails, because the path is for walking and the Vedika is the enclosing railing.

 

• a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv (Option 3): Giving the gateway to the Medhi and the platform to the Torana, and also misplacing the railing, contradicts the notes in three of the four pairs.

question: Which school of art is known for a purely Indian style of making Buddha images?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mathura school.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Mathura school of art, a purely Indian style, made Buddha images in the Kushana period, using red sandstone (मथुरा कला — भारतीय शैली)

 

• The Mathura school developed a purely Indian style of Buddha images, often using spotted red sandstone, in the Kushana period, as against the Greek-influenced Gandhara school.

 

• Both schools arose from the Mahayana acceptance of images, which turned the earlier symbols into human forms of the Buddha.

 

• Mathura workshops also made images of Jain Tirthankaras and Hindu deities, and Yaksha figures influenced the early Buddha type.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• SSC 2025 asked for the key difference between Mathura and Gandhara art.

 

• Gandhara used grey-blue schist and stucco.

 

• Gupta-age Sarnath images later became very refined.

 

• The Mathura school is also famed for its Kushana royal portrait statue of Kanishka, found at Mat near Mathura.

 

• Under the Kushanas the school at Mathura also made Bodhisattva images with a shaven head and the right hand raised in the abhaya gesture.

 

NOTE

 

• Gandhara school (Option 1): The Gandhara school is the Greek-influenced school known for realistic statues. Its Hellenistic features, such as wavy hair and heavy drapery, make it the opposite of a purely Indian style.

 

• Amaravati school (Option 2): Amaravati art flourished in the Krishna-Godavari region under the Satavahanas and is known for white marble reliefs on the stupa. It is not one of the two schools that came out of Mahayana in the notes.

 

• Nalanda school (Option 4): Nalanda sculpture belongs to the later Gupta-Pala period and is known for bronzes and stone images from the monastic university. It is not the Kushana school with a purely Indian style.

question:
Assertion (A): The Buddha sculptures of the Gandhara School show Hellenistic features.

Reason (R): The Buddha head from this school has curly hair and shows typical Hellenistic elements.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The curly hair and other Hellenistic elements of the Buddha head are exactly the features that show Greek influence in Gandhara sculpture, so both statements are true and R explains A (गांधार कला — यूनानी प्रभाव, घुंघराले बाल)

 

• The notes describe Gandhara art as shaped by Greek influence and known for realistic statues, and it flourished around Taxila and Peshawar under the Kushanas.

 

• The school arose as Mahayana encouraged images, and the Buddha was shown in Greco-Roman style with heavy drapery.

 

• This pair appeared in SSC 2025.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• This assertion and reason pair was asked in SSC 2025.

 

• Mathura art is the indigenous counterpart.

 

• The Kushana ruler Kanishka patronised both schools.

 

• The seated Buddha of Gandhara is often shown in a toga-like robe, with a moustache in some pieces and Apollo-like features.

 

• Gandhara has also given Bodhisattva statues, often wearing jewellery and a turban, which show the same Hellenistic influence.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The claim that R does not explain A fails, because the curly hair and Hellenistic elements in the head are the actual evidence of the Hellenistic features.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): The claim that R is false is wrong, since the Buddha head from Gandhara does have curly hair and other typical Hellenistic elements.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The claim that A is false is incorrect, because Gandhara sculptures are widely known for Hellenistic features. Since the reason also supports this fact, the assertion cannot be false.

question: 'Aniconism' in early Buddhist art refers to:
option_1: Depicting the Buddha only in human form
option_2: Worship of the Buddha through large stone images
option_3: Avoiding depiction of the Buddha in human form and showing him through symbols
option_4: Use of Greek styles for Buddha statues
solution_text:
The correct answer is Avoiding depiction of the Buddha in human form and showing him through symbols.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Aniconism means the prohibition or avoidance of depicting a divine figure in human form (anthropomorphic); instead the figure is shown through symbols and abstract motifs (अनिकोनिज़्म — प्रतीकों द्वारा बुद्ध का निरूपण)

 

• Aniconism is the avoidance of showing a divine figure in human form, using symbols and abstract motifs instead; in early Buddhist art the Buddha was shown by the wheel, tree, stupa, throne or footprints.

 

• This explains the symbols of the five great events: lotus and bull, horse, tree, wheel and stupa.

 

• The phase ended in the Kushana age with the human Buddha image, when Mahayana encouraged images.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sanchi and Bharhut belong to the aniconic phase.

 

• The earliest images of the Buddha are from Gandhara and Mathura.

 

• The notes define it as avoiding anthropomorphic depiction.

 

• Early Buddhist sculpture at Sanchi shows the Buddha's presence only by a Bodhi tree, an empty seat or an umbrella.

 

• The change from symbols to images is dated to the Kushana period, around the first and second centuries AD.

 

NOTE

 

• Depicting the Buddha only in human form (Option 1): Depicting the Buddha only in human form is the opposite of aniconism and describes the later Gandhara and Mathura images. Aniconism is the absence of human figures.

 

• Worship of the Buddha through large stone images (Option 2): Worship through large stone images belongs to the later phase after the Mahayana accepted image worship. Aniconism describes the earlier symbolic phase.

 

• Use of Greek styles for Buddha statues (Option 4): Use of Greek styles for Buddha statues describes Gandhara art, which depicts him in human form with Hellenistic features. It is not aniconism.

question: Which of the following Buddhist sites in Uttar Pradesh marks the spot where the Buddha preached his first sermon to five disciples?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sarnath.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sarnath, near Varanasi (Benares), in Uttar Pradesh is where the Buddha preached the first sermon to his five disciples, the event called Dharma Chakra Parivartan; the Dhamekh Stupa marks the spot (सारनाथ — प्रथम उपदेश, धमेख स्तूप)

 

• Sarnath near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh is the site of the first sermon to five disciples, called the Dharma Chakra Parivartan; the wheel is its symbol and the Dhamekh Stupa marks the place.

 

• The notes distinguish the four main places by state: Sarnath and Kushinagar in Uttar Pradesh, Bodh Gaya in Bihar and Lumbini in Nepal.

 

• Ashoka placed a lion-capital pillar at Sarnath, and the Gupta period saw a great Buddhist art school flourish there.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sarnath Lion Capital is the national emblem of India.

 

• Sarnath is also called Isipatana.

 

• Chinese pilgrims Fa-Hien and Xuanzang visited Sarnath.

 

• Fa-Hien visited India in the time of Chandragupta II of the Guptas and Xuanzang in the time of Harshavardhana.

 

• Sarnath, Bodh Gaya, Lumbini and Kushinagar form the group of four main Buddhist pilgrimage sites usually named together.

 

NOTE

 

• Kushinagar (Option 1): Kushinagar is in Uttar Pradesh but is the site of the Mahaparinirvana, the Buddha's death. The first sermon was preached elsewhere, at Sarnath.

 

• Bodh Gaya (Option 3): Bodh Gaya is the place of enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, and it lies in Bihar. It is neither in Uttar Pradesh nor the site of the first sermon.

 

• Rajagriha (Option 4): Rajagriha lies in Bihar and hosted the First Council. It is not in Uttar Pradesh and has no link to the first sermon.

question:
Consider the following statements about the Sangha:

1. Anyone could join, men and women, without caste restrictions.

2. The monks of the Sangha are called Bhikshus.

3. Admission to the Sangha was limited only to the Kshatriya varna.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sangha statements 1 and 2 are right, while statement 3 is false because admission was not limited to the Kshatriya varna; the notes say anyone, man or woman, could join and there were no caste restrictions (संघ — सभी जातियों के लिए खुला)

 

• The monks (Bhikshus) formed the Sangha, the third jewel of the Tri Ratna alongside the Buddha and the Dhamma.

 

• Caste-free membership set Buddhism apart from the Brahmanical order and helped it attract merchants and artisans.

 

• Hence any combination that includes statement 3 must be rejected.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Sangha followed rules recorded in the Vinaya Pitaka.

 

• Prajapati Gautami was the first woman admitted.

 

• The Sangha's decision-making followed the pattern of republican assemblies.

 

• The Buddha's own Sangha at Sarnath grew rapidly after the conversion of Yasa, a rich merchant's son, who brought fifty-four friends into the order.

 

• The first nuns' order also gave women of poorer classes an independent religious life, which the Vedic order did not offer.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): Statement 3 is false and statement 1 is true, so a pair holding the first and omitting the second does not work; the Sangha accepted men and women of all castes.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 2): A pair with the false statement 3 and the true statement 1 but without statement 2 on Bhikshus also fails; the notes call the monks Bhikshus.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 3): Taking all three together is impossible because the claim of Kshatriya-only entry contradicts the open admission policy explained in the notes.

question:
Consider the following statements about the First Buddhist Council:

1. It was held at Rajagriha in the Saptaparni cave.

2. Upali recited the Vinaya and Ananda the Sutta.

3. It was held about a century after the Buddha's death.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Only 1 and 2.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The First Buddhist Council was held at Rajagriha in the Saptaparni cave, where Upali recited the Vinaya and Ananda the Sutta, so statements 1 and 2 are right; statement 3 is wrong because it met right after the Buddha's death in 483 BC (प्रथम बौद्ध संगीति — राजगृह)

 

• Mahakasyapa presided and Ajatashatru gave support, which explains why the council could be held at the Magadhan capital.

 

• A century later the Second Council met at Vaishali, which is the source of the 'century' confusion in statement 3.

 

• The first-versus-second council distinction is a standard SSC trap.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The First Council was held in 483 BC and the Second in 383 BC.

 

• The Abhidhamma was prepared at the Third Council.

 

• Ajatashatru was a Haryanka king.

 

• The Second Council's separation from the first is why Buddhist tradition counts the first three or four councils as part of a connected series.

 

NOTE

 

• Only 2 and 3 (Option 1): That pair includes the false statement 3 and omits the true statement 1 about the Saptaparni cave at Rajagriha, so it fails.

 

• Only 1 and 3 (Option 3): That pair includes the false statement 3 and omits the true statement 2 about the recitations of Upali and Ananda, so it is not acceptable.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Accepting statement 3 contradicts the notes because the council was held immediately after the Buddha's death in 483 BC, not about a century later.

question: Gandhara and Mathura schools of Buddhist art, which began to show the Buddha in human form, flourished mainly under the patronage of which dynasty?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Kushanas.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Kushana dynasty, above all its greatest ruler Kanishka, patronised both Gandhara and Mathura art in the first to third centuries AD (गांधार और मथुरा कला — कुषाण संरक्षण)

 

• The Kushanas ruled a large empire in north-west and northern India, so both Gandhara in the north-west and Mathura in the Gangetic plain lay within their realm.

 

• Their patronage helped the Buddha to be portrayed in human form, which the notes connect to Mahayana and its image worship.

 

• Kanishka also patronised the Fourth Council, tying art and religion together.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Kushana capital was Purushapura, with Mathura as a second centre.

 

• Kanishka is associated with the Shaka era of 78 AD.

 

• Gold coins of the Kushanas show Buddha figures.

 

• The Kushanas also issued gold coins with images of Greek, Iranian and Indian deities, which shows the mixed cultural world in which Gandhara art grew.

 

NOTE

 

• Mauryas (Option 1): The Mauryas patronised Buddhism through Ashoka's pillars and stupas, but human Buddha images had not yet developed. Their art was symbolic and not the Gandhara or Mathura schools.

 

• Guptas (Option 2): The Guptas ruled later and are famous for the Sarnath school and Ajanta paintings. The Gandhara and Mathura schools were already established by Kushana times.

 

• Satavahanas (Option 3): The Satavahanas ruled in the Deccan and patronised the Amaravati art in the Krishna-Godavari region, which belongs to the south. It is not the dynasty linked with Gandhara and Mathura.
